moneyPages.title: Car Accident Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate your car accident settlement value using the multiplier method insurance adjusters use. Free calculator, no email required.
moneyPages.intro: Car accident claims combine two kinds of damages: your actual out-of-pocket losses (medical bills, lost wages, vehicle repair) and compensation for pain and suffering. Insurance adjusters typically use the multiplier method below as a starting point in negotiations — enter your numbers to see how it works.

faq.q: How accurate is a car accident settlement calculator?
faq.a: It gives a starting-point estimate using the same multiplier method insurance adjusters use, not a guaranteed outcome. Actual settlements depend on liability, insurance policy limits, and negotiation.

faq.q: Does fault percentage affect my settlement?
faq.a: Yes, and the exact effect depends on your state. Most states apply comparative negligence, reducing recovery proportionally by your fault percentage — some bar recovery entirely once fault crosses a threshold (typically 50% or 51%, and the exact cutoff varies by state). A handful of states (Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia, D.C.) use pure contributory negligence, where any fault at all can bar recovery, though real exceptions exist there too. Select your state above for the specific rule that applies — fault percentage is ultimately determined by a judge or jury, not by this estimate.

faq.q: How long after a car accident can I file a claim?
faq.a: Every state sets a statute of limitations for personal injury claims, typically 1 to 6 years from the accident date. Check your state's deadline — missing it usually bars the claim permanently.

sources.name: Insurance Information Institute — Auto Insurance Basics
Nolo — Car Accident Claims

moneyPages.title: Personal Injury Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate the value of your personal injury claim with the multiplier method. Covers medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering.
moneyPages.intro: Personal injury settlements generally cover two categories: economic damages (medical bills, lost income, property damage) and non-economic damages (pain and suffering). This calculator applies the multiplier method — the same approach insurance adjusters use as a negotiation starting point — to any type of injury claim.

faq.q: What counts as economic damages in a personal injury claim?
faq.a: Medical bills (past and future), lost wages, lost earning capacity, and property damage — losses with a specific dollar figure attached.

faq.q: What's the difference between economic and non-economic damages?
faq.a: Economic damages have a receipt or pay stub behind them. Non-economic damages (pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life) don't — they're estimated using methods like the multiplier.

faq.q: Do I need a lawyer to negotiate a personal injury settlement?
faq.a: Not always for minor claims, but insurers typically offer less to unrepresented claimants. For serious injuries or disputed liability, legal representation usually improves outcomes.

sources.name: American Bar Association — Personal Injury Basics
Justia — Personal Injury Law Center

moneyPages.title: Pain and Suffering Calculator — Free Multiplier Method Tool
moneyPages.metaDescription: Calculate estimated pain and suffering damages using the multiplier method. See exactly how insurers compute non-economic damages.
moneyPages.intro: Pain and suffering has no receipt — it's estimated. The multiplier method takes your total medical bills and lost wages and multiplies that figure by a number reflecting injury severity, typically between 1.5 and 5. This tool walks through that math step by step.

faq.q: How is pain and suffering calculated?
faq.a: The most common approach, the multiplier method, adds your medical expenses and lost wages, then multiplies the total by a severity factor (usually 1.5 to 5). A less common alternative, the per diem method, assigns a daily dollar value to your recovery period.

faq.q: What determines the multiplier used?
faq.a: Injury severity and permanence, recovery time, impact on daily life, and whether the injury is documented by objective medical evidence (imaging, surgery records) versus subjective complaints.

faq.q: Is pain and suffering taxable?
faq.a: Generally no — compensation for physical injury or sickness, including the pain and suffering portion, is excluded from federal taxable income under IRC Section 104(a)(2), with some exceptions for punitive damages.

sources.name: IRS — Publication 4345, Settlements
Nolo — Pain and Suffering Damages

moneyPages.title: Workers' Comp Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate your workers' compensation settlement based on medical costs, lost wages, and disability rating.
moneyPages.intro: Workers' compensation settlements work differently from injury lawsuits — they're typically no-fault, but pain and suffering usually isn't recoverable in the same way. This calculator estimates a settlement range based on medical costs, lost wages, and disability severity.

faq.q: Can I sue my employer instead of filing workers' comp?
faq.a: In most states, workers' comp is the exclusive remedy against your employer, meaning you generally can't also sue them for negligence. Exceptions exist for intentional harm or third-party liability (e.g., a defective machine made by another company).

faq.q: Does workers' comp cover pain and suffering?
faq.a: Generally no. Workers' comp covers medical treatment and a portion of lost wages, plus disability payments, but not pain and suffering the way a personal injury lawsuit would.

faq.q: How is a workers' comp settlement calculated?
faq.a: It's typically based on your average weekly wage, the state's compensation rate (often around two-thirds of wages), and your disability rating (percentage of impairment) as determined by a medical evaluation.

sources.name: U.S. Department of Labor — Workers' Compensation
Nolo — Workers' Comp Settlements

moneyPages.title: Dog Bite Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate your dog bite claim value based on medical bills, scarring, and pain and suffering.
moneyPages.intro: Dog bite claims usually settle through the owner's homeowners or renters insurance. Severity (puncture wounds, scarring, nerve damage, infection risk) drives the pain-and-suffering multiplier more than in most other injury types because bites often leave visible, permanent marks.

faq.q: Is the dog owner automatically liable for a bite?
faq.a: It depends on the state. Many states have strict liability laws holding owners responsible regardless of the dog's prior behavior; others follow a 'one bite rule' requiring proof the owner knew the dog was dangerous.

faq.q: Does scarring increase a dog bite settlement?
faq.a: Yes, significantly. Visible or permanent scarring, especially on the face or hands, typically pushes the pain-and-suffering multiplier toward the higher end of the range.

faq.q: What if the dog owner has no insurance?
faq.a: You may need to pursue the owner's personal assets directly, or in some cases file a claim under your own umbrella or renters/homeowners policy if applicable.

sources.name: CDC — Dog Bite Prevention
Nolo — Dog Bite Injury Claims

moneyPages.title: Medical Malpractice Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate a medical malpractice settlement, accounting for state damage caps on non-economic damages.
moneyPages.intro: Medical malpractice claims require proving a provider deviated from the accepted standard of care and that deviation caused harm — a higher bar than ordinary negligence. Many states also cap non-economic (pain and suffering) damages in malpractice cases specifically, which this calculator accounts for as a note, not a hard limit, since caps vary by state and are frequently litigated.

faq.q: Are there caps on medical malpractice settlements?
faq.a: Many states cap non-economic damages in malpractice cases specifically (commonly $250,000–$500,000, though amounts and rules vary widely and some states have no cap or have had caps struck down as unconstitutional). Economic damages like medical costs and lost wages are typically uncapped.

faq.q: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim?
faq.a: Statutes of limitations for malpractice are often shorter than for other injury claims and may start from when the harm was discovered rather than when it occurred — check your state's specific rule.

faq.q: Do I need an expert witness for a malpractice claim?
faq.a: Almost always. Most states require an affidavit or certificate of merit from a qualified medical expert just to file the claim, and expert testimony to prove the standard of care was breached.

sources.name: National Conference of State Legislatures — Medical Liability
Nolo — Medical Malpractice Claims

moneyPages.title: Wrongful Death Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate wrongful death damages including lost income, loss of companionship, and funeral costs.
moneyPages.intro: Wrongful death claims are brought by surviving family members or an estate representative, and damages typically include the deceased's lost future earnings, funeral and burial costs, and the family's loss of companionship, guidance, and support — categories this calculator estimates separately before combining them.

faq.q: Who can file a wrongful death claim?
faq.a: It varies by state, but typically a surviving spouse, children, or parents, or the personal representative of the deceased's estate on behalf of those beneficiaries.

faq.q: How is lost future income calculated in a wrongful death case?
faq.a: Based on the deceased's earning history, age, expected working years remaining, and benefits — often with input from an economist for larger claims.

faq.q: Is a wrongful death settlement taxable?
faq.a: Compensation for physical injury or death is generally excluded from federal taxable income, though punitive damages and interest on the settlement are typically taxable.

sources.name: Justia — Wrongful Death Claims
IRS — Publication 4345, Settlements

moneyPages.title: Whiplash Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate a whiplash injury settlement. See how treatment duration and documentation affect your claim value.
moneyPages.intro: Whiplash is one of the most disputed injury types in claims because it's a soft-tissue injury without a visible fracture — insurers often push back harder here than on injuries confirmed by imaging. Consistent medical treatment and documentation matter more for whiplash claims than almost any other injury type.

faq.q: Why do insurers dispute whiplash claims so often?
faq.a: Because whiplash is a soft-tissue injury that doesn't always show up on X-rays or MRIs, insurers sometimes argue it's minor or pre-existing. Consistent, well-documented treatment is the main counter.

faq.q: How long does whiplash take to settle?
faq.a: It's best to wait until you reach 'maximum medical improvement' (your condition has stabilized) before settling, since settling too early can leave future treatment costs uncompensated.

faq.q: Does a gap in treatment hurt my whiplash claim?
faq.a: Yes — gaps in treatment are one of the most common reasons insurers reduce whiplash settlement offers, since they suggest the injury wasn't serious enough to need ongoing care.

sources.name: Mayo Clinic — Whiplash Symptoms and Causes
Nolo — Whiplash Injury Claims

moneyPages.title: Slip and Fall Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate your slip and fall (premises liability) settlement based on medical costs and property owner negligence.
moneyPages.intro: Slip and fall claims fall under premises liability law, meaning you generally must show the property owner knew or should have known about a hazardous condition and failed to fix it or warn you. That negligence question often affects settlement value as much as the injury itself.

faq.q: Do I have to prove the property owner was negligent?
faq.a: Yes, generally. Unlike some claim types, premises liability usually requires showing the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and had a reasonable opportunity to address it.

faq.q: Does comparative negligence apply to slip and fall claims?
faq.a: Yes. If you were distracted, ignored a warning sign, or wearing inappropriate footwear, your settlement can be reduced by your percentage of fault, depending on your state's rule.

faq.q: What evidence helps a slip and fall claim?
faq.a: Photos of the hazard taken promptly, incident reports, surveillance footage, witness statements, and prompt medical treatment all strengthen a claim.

sources.name: OSHA — Slip, Trip, and Fall Prevention
Nolo — Slip and Fall Accident Claims

moneyPages.title: Lawsuit Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate a civil lawsuit settlement value covering economic damages plus pain and suffering.
moneyPages.intro: This general-purpose calculator applies the multiplier method used across most civil injury lawsuits, combining your documented economic losses with an estimated non-economic damages figure based on injury severity.

faq.q: What's the difference between a settlement and a judgment?
faq.a: A settlement is a negotiated agreement, usually reached before or during trial, with no admission of fault required. A judgment is a court's formal ruling after trial, which can be appealed.

faq.q: How long does a lawsuit take to settle?
faq.a: Anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on injury severity, whether liability is disputed, and how many parties are involved.

faq.q: Do most lawsuits settle before trial?
faq.a: Yes — the large majority of civil lawsuits, including personal injury cases, settle before reaching trial.

sources.name: U.S. Courts — Civil Cases
Justia — Civil Litigation

moneyPages.title: Motorcycle Accident Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate your motorcycle accident settlement. Motorcycle injuries tend to be more severe, affecting the pain and suffering multiplier.
moneyPages.intro: Motorcycle accidents tend to produce more severe injuries than car accidents at comparable speeds, since riders lack the protection of a vehicle frame — a factor that typically pushes the pain-and-suffering multiplier toward the higher end. Bias against riders from insurers and juries is also a real, well-documented factor in these claims.

faq.q: Why are motorcycle accident settlements sometimes lower than expected?
faq.a: Some insurers and juries hold unconscious bias against motorcyclists, assuming riders are more reckless — good documentation and, often, legal representation help counter this.

faq.q: Does not wearing a helmet reduce my settlement?
faq.a: In some states, yes — 'helmet laws' or comparative negligence rules can reduce compensation for head injuries if you weren't wearing a helmet, even where helmets aren't legally required.

faq.q: What damages are typical in a motorcycle accident claim?
faq.a: Medical bills, lost wages, motorcycle and gear repair/replacement, and pain and suffering — often weighted more heavily toward pain and suffering given injury severity.

sources.name: NHTSA — Motorcycle Safety
Nolo — Motorcycle Accident Claims

moneyPages.title: Truck Accident Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
moneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate your truck accident settlement. Commercial truck claims often involve multiple liable parties and higher policy limits.
moneyPages.intro: Commercial truck accidents differ from ordinary car accidents in two important ways: injuries tend to be more severe due to vehicle size and weight, and liability can extend beyond the driver to the trucking company, cargo loader, or maintenance contractor — often backed by much higher insurance policy limits.

faq.q: Who can be held liable in a truck accident?
faq.a: Potentially the driver, the trucking company (for hiring, training, or maintenance failures), a cargo loading company, or a parts manufacturer — multiple defendants are common.

faq.q: Do trucking companies have higher insurance limits?
faq.a: Yes, federal regulations require commercial trucks to carry significantly higher minimum liability coverage than passenger vehicles, often $750,000 or more depending on cargo type.

faq.q: Why do truck accident claims often take longer to resolve?
faq.a: Multiple potentially liable parties, federal trucking regulations (hours-of-service logs, maintenance records), and higher stakes for insurers all tend to extend the investigation and negotiation timeline.

sources.name: FMCSA — Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
Nolo — Truck Accident Claims

infoPages.title: What Determines a Car Accident Settlement Amount
infoPages.metaDescription: What actually drives a car accident settlement up or down: injury severity, medical bills, fault, and policy limits.
infoPages.h1: What Determines a Car Accident Settlement Amount
infoPages.body: There's no single 'average' car accident settlement that means much on its own — the range runs from a few thousand dollars for minor soft-tissue injuries to well into six or seven figures for catastrophic injuries. What moves the number: injury severity and permanence, total medical bills, lost income, clarity of fault, and available insurance policy limits. A settlement is capped by the at-fault driver's policy limit unless you have underinsured motorist coverage or other assets to pursue.

sources.name: Insurance Information Institute — Auto Insurance Basics
Insure.com — Minimum Car Insurance Coverage Levels

infoPages.title: How Injury Severity Drives Car Accident Settlement Amounts
infoPages.metaDescription: How treatment duration, injury severity, and policy limits set the ceiling and floor on a car accident settlement.
infoPages.h1: How Injury Severity Drives Car Accident Settlement Amounts
infoPages.body: Settlement amounts scale closely with injury severity and treatment duration. Minor soft-tissue injuries with a few weeks of treatment settle far lower than injuries requiring surgery, hospitalization, or ongoing care. Policy limits are the practical ceiling in most cases — a driver with only state-minimum liability coverage caps what you can recover from them directly, regardless of how severe your injuries are.

sources.name: Insurance Information Institute — Auto Insurance Basics
Insure.com — Minimum Car Insurance Coverage Levels

infoPages.title: Why There's No Fixed Average Pain and Suffering Settlement
infoPages.metaDescription: Pain and suffering is calculated as a multiplier of economic damages, not a flat average — see how the multiplier method works.
infoPages.h1: Why There's No Fixed Average Pain and Suffering Settlement
infoPages.body: Pain and suffering settlements are usually expressed as a multiplier of your economic damages (medical bills plus lost wages), typically 1.5x for minor injuries up to 5x for severe, permanent injuries. There's no fixed dollar 'average' that applies across injury types, since the multiplier is designed to scale with severity rather than produce a flat number.

sources.name: Insurance Information Institute — Auto Insurance Basics
Nolo — Car Accident Claims

infoPages.title: What Determines a Slip and Fall Settlement
infoPages.metaDescription: Why slip and fall settlements vary more than car accident claims, and what proving negligence has to do with it.
infoPages.h1: What Determines a Slip and Fall Settlement
infoPages.body: Slip and fall settlements vary more than car accident settlements for a structural reason: you have to prove the property owner's negligence, not just that you were injured. A slip and fall with clear negligence (a known, unaddressed hazard) and serious injury can settle well; a similar injury with disputed negligence often settles for far less, or not at all.

sources.name: Nolo — What Is a Premises Liability Claim?
Nolo — How to Prove Liability in a Slip and Fall Case

infoPages.title: Average Dog Bite Settlement Amount
infoPages.metaDescription: Typical dog bite settlement ranges, and how scarring and permanent injury affect the payout.
infoPages.body: Dog bite settlements skew higher than many injury types of comparable medical cost because of scarring and disfigurement, which juries and insurers weigh heavily in the pain-and-suffering multiplier — especially for facial or hand injuries. Most dog bite claims are paid through the owner's homeowners or renters insurance liability coverage.

sources.name: Triple-I (III) — Spotlight on Dog Bite Liability

infoPages.title: What Affects a Medical Malpractice Settlement Amount
infoPages.metaDescription: Why medical malpractice settlements run higher than typical injury claims, and how state damage caps can reduce the total.
infoPages.h1: What Affects a Medical Malpractice Settlement Amount
infoPages.body: Medical malpractice settlements tend to run higher than most other injury claims because the underlying harm is often severe (surgical errors, misdiagnosis, birth injuries), but many states cap the non-economic (pain and suffering) portion specifically for malpractice cases, which can significantly reduce the total compared to what a similar injury would recover in a standard negligence claim.

sources.name: NCSL — Summary of Medical Liability / Medical Malpractice Laws

infoPages.title: Average Workers' Comp Settlement Amount
infoPages.metaDescription: Typical workers' compensation settlement ranges, based on wage rate and disability percentage.
infoPages.body: Workers' comp settlements are calculated differently from injury lawsuits — there's no pain-and-suffering multiplier. Instead, the amount is driven mainly by your average weekly wage, your state's compensation rate, and your permanent disability rating as determined by a medical evaluation.

sources.name: AllLaw (Nolo network) — How Much Do Workers' Compensation Benefits Pay?

infoPages.title: How Is Pain and Suffering Calculated?
infoPages.metaDescription: The multiplier method and per diem method explained — how insurers and lawyers actually calculate pain and suffering.
infoPages.h1: How Is Pain and Suffering Calculated?
infoPages.body: Two methods dominate: the multiplier method (economic damages × a severity factor, usually 1.5-5) and the per diem method (a fixed dollar amount per day of recovery). The multiplier method is more common in practice, especially for insurance adjuster negotiations. Neither method is a legal requirement — both are negotiation tools, and actual settlements depend on the specific facts of the case.

sources.name: Insurance Information Institute — Auto Insurance Basics
Nolo — Car Accident Claims

eeocMoneyPages.title: Discrimination Lawsuit Settlement Calculator — Free Estimate
eeocMoneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate how much you could sue for in a workplace discrimination lawsuit — back pay, front pay, and compensatory/punitive damages by claim type.
eeocMoneyPages.intro: Workplace discrimination lawsuits — based on race, sex, age, disability, religion, or national origin — don't settle like an injury claim. There's no pain-and-suffering multiplier; instead, the law splits your recovery into an uncapped bucket (back pay, front pay) and, depending on which law applies to your claim, a capped bucket (compensatory and punitive damages). This calculator walks through both, using the same statutory structure as our more detailed EEOC settlement calculator — use this version for a quick estimate by claim type, or the EEOC calculator if you already know which federal or state law applies.

faq.q: How much can I sue for in a discrimination lawsuit?
faq.a: It depends entirely on which law applies. Back pay and front pay are never capped and depend on your actual lost earnings. Compensatory and punitive damages are capped by employer size under federal law (Title VII, ADA) at $50,000–$300,000 combined, uncapped under California's FEHA, and unavailable at all under the ADEA (age discrimination), which instead allows liquidated damages that can double your back pay if the violation was willful.

faq.q: Does it matter if my discrimination claim is based on race, age, or disability?
faq.a: Yes — the applicable law changes the math. Race, sex, religion, and national origin claims fall under Title VII; disability claims under the ADA (same damages caps as Title VII); age claims under the ADEA (no compensatory/punitive damages, but liquidated damages for willful violations); and in California, FEHA covers all of the above with no damages cap at all.

faq.q: What's a typical discrimination lawsuit settlement range?
faq.a: There's no single average — documented cases with clear lost wages and moderate emotional distress often settle in the tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands; egregious, well-documented cases with strong evidence and no damages cap (e.g., under California FEHA) can exceed $1 million. The employer's size and which law applies drive most of the variation.

faq.q: Do I need to file with the EEOC before suing?
faq.a: For federal claims (Title VII, ADA, ADEA), yes — you generally must file a charge with the EEOC (or a state fair employment agency) and receive a 'right to sue' letter before filing in court. California FEHA claims go through the state's Civil Rights Department instead.

sources.name: EEOC — Notice 915.002, Compensatory and Punitive Damages
EEOC — Filing a Charge of Discrimination

eeocMoneyPages.title: EEOC Settlement Calculator — Back Pay, Front Pay & Damages Caps
eeocMoneyPages.metaDescription: Estimate an employment discrimination settlement: back pay, front pay, and compensatory/punitive damages under Title VII, ADA, ADEA, or California FEHA.
eeocMoneyPages.intro: Employment discrimination settlements don't use the injury multiplier method — they follow a statutory structure that depends on which law applies. Back pay and front pay are never capped. Compensatory and punitive damages under Title VII and the ADA are capped by employer size (42 U.S.C. § 1981a), fixed at 1991 levels. The ADEA (age discrimination) has no compensatory/punitive damages at all — it uses back pay plus liquidated damages for willful violations. California's FEHA has no cap on any damages. Select your law type below to apply the right formula.

faq.q: Are EEOC settlement caps the same for every type of discrimination?
faq.a: No. Title VII (race, sex, religion, national origin) and the ADA (disability) share the same compensatory + punitive damages caps under 42 U.S.C. § 1981a, from $50,000 to $300,000 depending on employer size. The ADEA (age discrimination) doesn't use these caps at all — it has no compensatory or punitive damages, only back pay and liquidated damages. California FEHA claims have no statutory cap.

faq.q: Does the settlement cap apply to back pay and front pay?
faq.a: No. The § 1981a cap covers only compensatory (e.g. emotional distress) and punitive damages combined. Back pay is equitable relief under Title VII itself, and the Supreme Court held in Pollard v. E.I. du Pont (2001) that front pay is not part of the capped damages either — both are uncapped, on top of whatever the capped bucket totals.

faq.q: Can I get punitive damages against a government employer?
faq.a: No. Punitive damages under 42 U.S.C. § 1981a are unavailable against public/government employers, regardless of employer size. Compensatory damages and back/front pay remain available.

faq.q: Have the EEOC damages caps ever been raised for inflation?
faq.a: No. The caps were set in the Civil Rights Act of 1991 and have never been indexed for inflation — $300,000 in 1991 has roughly half the purchasing power today.

faq.q: What's different about age discrimination (ADEA) claims?
faq.a: The ADEA doesn't provide compensatory or punitive damages at all. Instead, a plaintiff can recover back pay, front pay, and — if the violation was willful — liquidated damages equal to the back pay amount (effectively doubling it).

sources.name: EEOC — Notice 915.002, Compensatory and Punitive Damages
Pollard v. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co., 532 U.S. 843 (2001)
